auth.notes: Standard AWS IoT device-shadow MQTT with per-thing X.509 certificate credentials (AWS IoT Core mutual TLS); topics $aws/things/<thingName>/shadow/get, /shadow/update and their /accepted siblings confirmed as strings in the Rabbit Air 2 app binary. Recorded for completeness — consumers should use the LAN protocol, not this.

endpoints.name: GraphQL account API
endpoints.notes: Operation names are read as users/* strings from the Rabbit Air 2 app binary (confidence: medium — app-derived, no live capture). Account/auth: login_by_pass, register_user_send_code, register_user_by_otp, activate_account, check_pin_code, send_email_pin, reset_password_or_activate, deleteAccount, restoreAccount, update_aws_token, setUserFirebaseToken, removeUserFirebaseToken. Device management: serialByMac (serial → cloud lookup during provisioning), unit_create, unit_delete, unit_set_primary, editUnitNameAndLocation, reserve_thing_name_v2, getThingShadow, getUserFullInfo, updateRegion, location_list, updateScheduleSettings, updateScheduleName. Shop/account extras (Shopify-backed): test_shop, getAllFilters, getAllSkins, setUnitSkin, updateUserShopifyInfo, shopify_addresses_delete. A bare `generateUserKey` operation (no users/ prefix) also appears; it is the user-key generation flow, see device.setup.credentials. Recorded for completeness — consumers should use the LAN protocol.

cloud.failure_mode: None for local control: the LAN protocol on UDP 9009 is independent of the cloud. Losing the cloud removes remote (out-of-home) control, account/device management, Alexa/Google linkage, and OTA firmware delivery.
hosts: GraphQL account API at path /graphql.json (package:graphql present; production host string not isolated in the app binary — 'rabbitair.skilap.org' appears once as a candidate host, role unconfirmed, low confidence)
cloud.notes: The app mirrors purifier state through the AWS IoT Device Shadow service (the app's shadow model). Everything the shadow carries is also readable locally via cmd 4.
cloud.vendor_service: Rabbit Air cloud (AWS IoT Core + account API)

child_lock_off.description: Release the child lock: cmd 4 with data {"lock": false}.

child_lock_on.description: Engage the child lock: cmd 4 with data {"lock": true}.

get_info.description: Device info: cmd 255. Reply data carries name (Thing ID), mac, mcu (Wi-Fi firmware version), build (firmware build date), time, uptime counters (uptime / mup / wup / iup / cup), fv (main-board firmware) and rssi as a {cur,min,max,avg} object — note that is a different shape from the hourly-averaged integer `rssi` in get_state.

get_state.description: Poll the full purifier state: cmd 4 with no `data`. This is THE state poll — every entity below reads its value out of this reply's `data` object, and every state_mapping path is relative to that object's root (`power` means reply data.power). Reply fields are all optional in practice; the complete field table is rabbit_air_protocol.state_fields.

returns.description: Purifier on/off. The Power switch reads this.
returns.name: power

returns.description: 0 Auto / 1 Pollen / 2 Manual. The Mode select reads this.
returns.name: mode

returns.description: 0 SuperSilent (auto modes only, read-only) / 1 Silent / 2 Low / 3 Medium / 4 High / 5 Turbo. The Fan Speed number reads this.
returns.name: speed

returns.description: Air quality 0-4 (Lowest/Low/Medium/High/Highest); BioGS (model 2) reports 1-5 — subtract 1. The Air Quality sensor reads this.
returns.name: quality

returns.description: Negative ion generator on/off. The Ionizer switch reads this.
returns.name: ionizer

returns.description: Child lock on/off. The Child Lock switch reads this.
returns.name: lock

returns.description: Remaining filter lifetime in minutes. The Filter Life sensor reads this.
returns.name: filter_life

returns.description: Wi-Fi RSSI averaged over an hour. The Wi-Fi RSSI sensor reads this.
returns.name: rssi

returns.description: 1 MinusA2 / 2 BioGS / 3 A3 — needed to apply the BioGS quality offset.
returns.name: model

ionizer_off.description: Disable the negative ion generator: cmd 4 with data {"ionizer": false}.

ionizer_on.description: Enable the negative ion generator: cmd 4 with data {"ionizer": true}.

set_mode.description: Set the operating mode: cmd 4 with data {"mode": N}. One caller parameter — the mode the user picked.
set_mode.example_notes: Manual mode, built from mode=2 substituted into the body.

set_speed.description: Set the manual fan speed: cmd 4 with data {"mode": 2, "speed": N}. The body pins mode=2 deliberately — the vendor client treats a speed change under Auto/Pollen as an implicit switch to Manual, and stating it makes the write deterministic and leaves this command with the ONE caller parameter a number control can fill.
set_speed.example_notes: Medium speed, built from speed=3 substituted into the body.

speed.description: 1 Silent / 2 Low / 3 Medium / 4 High / 5 Turbo. 0 (SuperSilent) is read-only, reported by auto modes — not settable here.

time_sync.description: Read the device clock: cmd 9, reply data.ts in seconds. Must precede the first authenticated command — the renderer computes the clock offset from this reply and stamps every later request's `ts` with the extrapolated device time (see rabbit_air_protocol.handshake).

turn_off.description: Power the purifier off: cmd 4 with data {"power": false}.

turn_on.description: Power the purifier on: cmd 4 with data {"power": true}.

methods.notes: When the unit has a Thing ID (vendor cloud flow), the mDNS hostname IS the Thing ID (AWS IoT thing name), e.g. "abcdef1234_123456789012345678.local" (vendor library README). HARDWARE-VERIFIED 2026-08-15 for a local-only provisioning (no cloud, no Thing ID — cmd 255 data.name stays ""): the unit advertises service instance AND hostname "RabbitAir-<WIFI MAC>" — e.g. RabbitAir-A1B2C3D4E5F6.local for a unit whose Wi-Fi MAC is A1:B2:C3:D4:E5:F6 — with a single TXT record "id=A1B2C3D4E5F6" (the MAC, uppercase, no separators). Consumers keying the LAN credential by hostname must handle this fallback: the key scope is derivable at provisioning time from cmd 255's data.mac ("RabbitAir-" + mac.upper() minus colons) even when data.name is empty. Resolving the service/hostname yields the IP to send UDP 9009 traffic to. Home Assistant discovers the device by exactly this zeroconf service type.

The purifier advertises the Rabbit Air GATT service whenever its BLE radio is up — as "RabbitAirSetup" while unprovisioned (setup mode) and as "RabbitAir" once provisioned. A BLE scan match means "Rabbit Air purifier"; the advertised NAME tells you which mode it is in. BLE is a full alternate transport for the same command envelope (plaintext during setup, user-key-encrypted after) — see rabbit_air_ble.

device.name: Rabbit Air MinusA2 (SPA-700A/SPA-780A) / A3 (SPA-1000N) / BioGS 2.0 (SPA-550A/SPA-625A)
device.notes:
Rabbit Air's Wi-Fi-enabled purifiers speak an encrypted JSON-over-UDP LAN protocol on port 9009. Rabbit Air is an ACTIVE company; the value of this spec is that the LAN protocol is fully local — no cloud account, no internet round-trip — and the vendor's own Apache-2.0 library implements it. The Home Assistant core integration (local_polling) drives the purifier entirely over this LAN protocol.
Coverage: MinusA2 second generation (SPA-700A / SPA-780A Wi-Fi models), A3 (SPA-1000N) and BioGS 2.0 (SPA-550A / SPA-625A). The state model in the vendor library carries an explicit `model` field (1 = MinusA2, 2 = BioGS, 3 = A3). FIRST-GENERATION MinusA2 (older hardware revision, pre-"Rabbit Air 2" app) does NOT speak this protocol — the app reports "your device is not supported" and the HA integration cannot connect; that generation used a different, undocumented interface.
Security model: all LAN traffic after provisioning is AES-128-CBC with a per-device 16-byte "user key" (access token). The key is generated on-device and revealed to the owner through the official app (Rename device screen, or by tapping "Serial Number" repeatedly on the edit screen in older app versions). A request carries a device-clock timestamp (anti-replay); the client learns the clock via cmd 9. Datagrams larger than one UDP payload are not used; the same protocol is also reachable over TCP 9009 with a 2-byte little-endian length prefix per message (vendor TcpClient).
Cloud dependency: none for control. The Rabbit Air 2 app additionally talks to Rabbit Air's cloud (AWS IoT Core device shadow over MQTTS, GraphQL account API, ota.rabbitair.com for firmware) for remote access, account features and OTA — see the `cloud` block. Local control keeps working if the cloud dies.

openness.notes: Unusual case: the vendor itself published the LAN client library (python-rabbitair, Apache-2.0) and wrote the Home Assistant integration, so the local protocol is documented_api-by-reference-implementation — the library source, not this file, is authoritative for constants. reverse_engineered is still true because the Wi-Fi provisioning flow (BLE-assisted / AP-mode) is NOT published — it was recovered here from static analysis of the Rabbit Air 2 app's Dart snapshot and is recorded in setup.methods, rabbit_air_protocol.setup_commands and rabbit_air_ble.

issued_to_client: user key / access token (32 hex chars = 16 bytes)
credentials.notes: The LAN credential is a per-device 16-byte user key. The app settled how it is born: the APP generates it — 32 uppercase hex characters drawn from dart:math Random — and pushes it to the unit with cmd 5, data {"type":4,"value":"<32 hex>"} (feature-gated on firmware: mcu >= 24 on ESP32 units, >= 2.2 on Inventek; older units report "User key write not supported"). A third-party provisioner can therefore mint the key itself during setup and needs nothing from the vendor cloud. On units set up before user keys existed, the official app offers "Tap for setup user key" to run the same push after the fact. The owner can also READ an existing key out of the official app: device control page > three-dot menu > Rename > tap the device name to expand — the screen reveals Thing ID and User key (older app versions: Edit screen, tap "Serial Number" several times). Never record a real key in this repo — the spec documents the shape only.
stored_on_device: user key (16-byte AES key, generated client-side and pushed via cmd 5 type 4)
AWS IoT thing certificate (cloud path, cmd 5 types 0-3 — optional)

factory_reset.effect: Clears Wi-Fi credentials and cloud binding, returning the unit to its unprovisioned state (BLE advertising / setup AP). Exact button procedure varies by model and is described in the printed manuals (Wi-Fi/reset control on the unit's panel); not captured in this project — stated at low confidence rather than guessed.

ble.protocol: Rabbit Air setup — cleartext JSON command envelope over GATT (see rabbit_air_ble)

methods.description: Preferred path in the Rabbit Air 2 app (its "mobile" connection method). The phone scans for the setup-mode peripheral — advertised name "RabbitAirSetup", GATT service 366048ae-9f36-43cf-8004-010c0c9fa52e — connects, negotiates MTU 515, and speaks the cleartext setup command set (rabbit_air_protocol.setup_commands) through the single command characteristic 53ef7d7d-c244-42bd-9064-a1569a521ca9 (write-with-response, INDICATIONS on the same characteristic — verified on hardware; the app code read "notifications"), framed and chunked exactly as rabbit_air_ble describes. Conversation: cmd 255 + cmd 4 (info/state sanity check), cmd 0 (read network settings — doubles as the device's own Wi-Fi scan list), cmd 1 (join network — ssid/passphrase/security), cmd 5 type 4 (push a client-generated user key), cmd 3 (set module name), cmd 2 (leave setup mode). The unit then joins Wi-Fi and appears on the LAN as _rabbitair._udp.local — allow MINUTES, not seconds: the verified unit held ip 0.0.0.0 in cmd 0 for ~4 minutes after cmd 2 before it associated and took a DHCP lease. The vendor app additionally pushes AWS IoT certificates (cmd 5 types 0-3) for cloud binding — optional; skip for local-only provisioning.

steps.action: Power the purifier and hold Speed/Wireless until the wireless LED blinks — it advertises 'RabbitAirSetup' over BLE.
Scan for service 366048ae-9f36-43cf-8004-010c0c9fa52e (name 'RabbitAirSetup'), connect, request MTU 515.
cmd 255 get_info + cmd 4 state_get (retry up to 5x, 1 s apart) — confirms the channel and reads model/mcu.
cmd 0 read_network_settings — re-poll until data.networks is non-empty; present the SSID list.
Pick the SSID and enter its passphrase.
cmd 1 join_network, data {"ssid":...,"passphrase":...,"security":<int>} — security is echoed from the chosen networks[] entry (3 = WPA2-PSK observed on hardware; see setup_commands).
Generate the user key client-side (32 uppercase hex chars = 16 bytes) and push it: cmd 5, data {"type":4,"value":"<32 hex>"}.
steps.notes: Feature-gate on firmware: user-key write needs mcu >= 24 on ESP32 units / >= 2.2 on Inventek units — older firmware rejects it ('User key write not supported' in the app).

steps.action: Optional: cmd 3 set_module_name; cmd 5 types 0-3 push AWS IoT/HTTPS certificates (cloud binding only — skip for local-only use).
cmd 2 leave_ap_mode — the unit joins the Wi-Fi network.
steps.expect: Unit appears on the LAN advertising _rabbitair._udp.local.; verify with an encrypted cmd 9 + cmd 4 under the new user key. On the verified unit this took ~4 minutes (cmd 0 reported ip 0.0.0.0 the whole wait) — keep watching rather than failing fast.

timing.chunk_size_rule: negotiated MTU - 5 (the app's default before negotiation is 512)
timing.network_list_note: cmd 0 is re-polled (up to 15x) until data.networks is non-empty

causes: Unit is not in setup mode — hold Speed/Wireless until the wireless LED blinks.
Unit is already provisioned — it advertises as 'RabbitAir' (still matches service 366048ae-…); factory-reset to re-provision.
The unit is NOT in setup mode (already keyed) — a provisioned unit drops all cleartext commands and intermittently 0x87s the writes. Hold the wireless button until the LED blinks.
Observed on keyed hardware 2026-08-15: no cleartext command (255/4/7/0/1) is answered or acted on in this state, and post-setup cmd 1/2 return {"id":…,"error":true} over the encrypted channel too.
troubleshooting.symptom: Writes are rejected with ATT application error 0x87, or accepted but never answered

causes: MTU negotiation did not reach 515, so the 510-byte chunks exceeded the real ATT MTU.
The unit left setup mode (timeout or completed join).
troubleshooting.symptom: Command round trip times out (7 s) or the connection drops mid-setup

causes: Firmware too old — user-key write requires mcu >= 24 (ESP32) / >= 2.2 (Inventek).
Give it minutes first — the verified join took ~4 minutes.
Wrong passphrase or a 5 GHz-only BSSID; re-enter setup mode and re-run cmd 1 with the corrected credentials.
troubleshooting.symptom: cmd 1 acked but the unit never gets an IP (cmd 0 keeps reporting 0.0.0.0)

methods.verification_notes: Replayed against hardware 2026-08-15 (MinusA2 gen2, mcu 2.2.8): scan → connect → MTU 515 → enable INDICATIONS on the command characteristic → cleartext cmd 255, 4, 7, 0 (poll), 1, 5 type 4, 2 — every reply arrived as documented, framed 2-byte-LE-length-prefixed. Every command's reply is a bare {"id":<echo>} ack for the writes and {"id":…,"data":{…}} for the reads; failures surface as {"id":<echo>,"error":true} (observed when cmd 1/2 were re-sent AFTER setup completed — the setup command set is only accepted while the unit is in setup mode). One correction to that reading: the characteristic's server-to-client leg is INDICATIONS (properties 0x28 = write + indicate), not notifications — and its CCCD already reads 0x0002 on a fresh connection (indications enabled by default), but clients should still write the CCCD explicitly. A KEYED unit (already provisioned, not in setup mode) does not answer cleartext at all: writes are intermittently rejected with ATT application error 0x87 and otherwise accepted-and-dropped, so a setup probe that gets silence/0x87 means "not in setup mode".

methods.description: AP-mode fallback (the app's "local" connection method): the device hosts an open setup AP (SSID prefix "rabbitair_"); after joining it, the phone speaks the SAME cleartext setup command set as the BLE path — one JSON envelope per UDP datagram to 192.168.10.1:9009 (or TCP 9009 with the 2-byte little-endian length prefix). The app first resolves the fixed hostname rabbitair-setup.local via mDNS and falls back to the fixed gateway IP; the command sequence is identical to the BLE method (cmd 255/4 → 0 → 1 → 5 → 3 → 2), and cmd 2 "leave AP mode" closes the AP at the end. Transport confirmed from the app (wifi_iot joins the rabbitair_* SSID, then UDP/TCP 9009); 192.168.10.1:9009 independently corroborated by yepher/RabbiteAirProtocol's iOS research.

steps.action: Put the purifier in AP/setup mode (Wi-Fi button on the unit; app-guided).
Join the open rabbitair_* AP from OS Wi-Fi settings.
Resolve rabbitair-setup.local via mDNS or use 192.168.10.1; run the same cleartext command sequence as the BLE method (cmd 255/4 → 0 → 1 → 5 type 4 → 3 → 2) over UDP 9009.
steps.expect: cmd 2 leaves AP mode; the unit joins Wi-Fi and appears on the LAN advertising _rabbitair._udp.local.

methods.description: Third connection method in the app: router push-button WPS join. The app then skips cmd 0/1 (no credentials cross the phone) and cmd 2, running only the naming/certificate steps (cmd 3/5). Which transport carries those commands in WPS mode has not been traced; recorded for completeness — prefer the BLE method.

setup.notes:
The purifier must be joined to Wi-Fi once. The full provisioning protocol is documented below — originally recovered by static analysis of the Rabbit Air 2 app's Dart snapshot, and since REPLAYED AGAINST HARDWARE (2026-08-15, MinusA2 gen2, Wi-Fi module mcu 2.2.8): the BLE method below ran end-to-end exactly as written and the unit came up on the LAN under a client-generated user key. The app offers three connection methods — BLE-assisted ("mobile"), AP-mode ("local") and WPS — and the first two converge on the SAME command channel: the JSON {id, cmd, data} envelope of the LAN protocol, sent in CLEARTEXT during setup (no `ts` field, no AES — encryption is only switched on afterwards, once a user key exists). Over BLE the envelope is framed and chunked per rabbit_air_ble; over the setup AP it is one datagram per message to 192.168.10.1:9009, byte-identical to the LAN protocol minus encryption.
A local-only provisioner needs NO cloud: generate the 16-byte user key CLIENT-side (32 uppercase hex chars), push it with cmd 5 type 4, and the unit is fully controllable over LAN and BLE without any Rabbit Air account — VERIFIED: the unit provisioned this way answers encrypted cmd 9/255/4 over UDP 9009 and over BLE. Consequence of skipping the cloud flow: the unit has no Thing ID (cmd 255 data.name stays ""), and its mDNS hostname falls back to "RabbitAir-<WIFI MAC>" (see discovery). The vendor app's own flow additionally does cloud work (serial QR scan, GraphQL serialByMac / reserveThingNameV2, and pushing AWS IoT certificates with cmd 5 types 0-3) — that binds the unit to the vendor cloud and is optional for local control.

rejoin.notes: No documented in-place credential update; treat a router change as reset-and-reprovision through the app.

testing.notes: 2026-08-15: the BLE provisioning flow was executed end-to-end against a real MinusA2 (model 1, Wi-Fi module mcu 2.2.8): cleartext cmd 255/4/7/0 reads, cmd 1 join, cmd 5 type 4 user-key push, cmd 2 leave — all answered as documented. Post-join, the LAN protocol was driven over UDP 9009 with the pushed key (cmd 9 clock sync, cmd 255 info, cmd 4 state) and the ENCRYPTED BLE control transport was exercised the same way. The softap_udp and WPS methods remain unreplayed; the LAN state-set surface is exercised only as far as reads. Join latency observation: after cmd 2 the unit held ip 0.0.0.0 for ~4 minutes before associating and taking a DHCP lease — a client should keep watching, not declare failure.

entities.name: Fan Speed
entities.notes: Manual-mode speeds 1-5 (Silent/Low/Medium/High/Turbo). A state of 0 — SuperSilent, reported by the Auto/Pollen modes — is read-only and sits below this control's minimum; display it as-is rather than clamping. Setting a speed also sends mode=2 (see the set_speed command).

entities.name: Air Quality
entities.notes: 0-4. BioGS 2.0 units (model 2) report 1-5 and the vendor library subtracts 1 — apply the same offset, keyed on the reply's `model` field.

entities.name: Filter Life
entities.notes: Minutes remaining; pair with the filter_replacement flag in the same reply, which is the actionable alert when life runs out.

entities.name: Wi-Fi RSSI
entities.notes: Hourly average per the vendor state model; the get_info command returns a {cur,min,max,avg} snapshot instead.

example_wire.description: cmd 255 get_info, cleartext, as framed on BLE. id is a per-client counter starting at 0.
example_wire.note: 13+2 = 15 bytes fit one chunk, so this example is a single write; a cmd 1 join message with a long passphrase crosses one chunk boundary at 510 bytes.

framing.description: Every request/response payload (the plaintext-or-encrypted envelope bytes — the same bytes one UDP datagram would carry) is prefixed with a 2-byte LITTLE-ENDIAN uint16 length of the PAYLOAD ONLY (prefix not counted), then split into consecutive chunks of (negotiated MTU - 5) bytes. The app requests MTU 515, so chunks are 510 bytes; its pre-negotiation default chunk is 512. Each chunk is one GATT write (with response), sent sequentially.
framing.reassembly: Indications arrive in the same chunking (hardware-verified: ATT Handle Value Indications, which the client's ATT layer confirms). The first indication of a message starts with the 2-byte LE total-payload length; accumulate chunk bodies (skipping the 2-byte prefix of the first chunk) until that many payload bytes have arrived — that is the complete response, which then goes through the normal decrypt/JSON path. Indications shorter than 2 bytes are ignored. The app waits at most 7 s for a complete response.

advertised_names.provisioned: RabbitAir — after setup; the app matches this name plus the unit's BT MAC. Note (hardware-observed): a provisioned unit's ADVERTISING data carried no local name at all — only the service UUID; the name 'RabbitAir' came from the GAP Device Name characteristic (0x2A00) read after connect.

gatt.operations: Single characteristic for both directions: the client WRITES requests (write-WITH-response) and subscribes to INDICATIONS (not notifications — properties 0x28, hardware-verified) for responses; the client must send ATT confirmations. No BLE pairing/bonding.

off_wifi_access.security_note: Corollary: while a unit sits in setup mode it discloses state, identity and its Wi-Fi scan results to ANY BLE client in range, and accepts cmd 1 (join network) from anyone — the provisioning window is unauthenticated by design. Keep setup mode short.
off_wifi_access.summary: The purifier's BLE radio is up whether or not it has joined a WLAN, so state/info is reachable with the device entirely off Wi-Fi. A unit in SETUP mode answers the cleartext command set with no credentials at all — cmd 255 (name, MAC, firmware, uptimes), cmd 4 (full live state: power, mode, speed, air quality, filter life, ...), cmd 0 (its own Wi-Fi scan list), cmd 7 — the vendor app's own setup flow reads cmd 255 + cmd 4 exactly this way before any key exists. A PROVISIONED unit keeps advertising ("RabbitAir") and accepts the full command set over BLE encrypted under its user key — the vendor app's CurrentDeviceProvider does bluetoothConnect + setEncrypted for local control independent of the LAN — VERIFIED 2026-08-15: after a local-only provisioning (no cloud), encrypted cmd 9/255/0/4 ran over BLE under the pushed key with the unit reachable/unreachable on Wi-Fi alike. The one closed case: a keyed unit whose key you don't have — there is no BLE pairing/bonding to fall back on and every command needs the AES key; VERIFIED: such a unit answers no cleartext command and intermittently rejects the writes with ATT application error 0x87.

provisioning_over_ble.summary: During setup the framed payloads are the CLEARTEXT {"id","cmd","data"} envelopes of rabbit_air_protocol.setup_commands (no ts, no AES). Order in the app: cmd 255 + cmd 4 (info/state, 5 retries 1 s apart) → cmd 0 (network list; re-poll up to 15x until networks[] non-empty) → cmd 1 (join network) → cmd 5 type 4 (push client-generated user key) → cmd 3 (set name) → cmd 2 (leave setup mode). Cloud-only extras (cmd 5 types 0-3 certificates) can be skipped. Afterwards the unit joins Wi-Fi; verify over LAN with an encrypted cmd 9 + cmd 4 under the new key.

rabbit_air_ble.verification_notes: 2026-08-15, MinusA2 gen2 (Wi-Fi module mcu 2.2.8): full cleartext provisioning conversation and the post-setup ENCRYPTED command set (cmd 9 clock sync, 255 info, 0 network, 4 state) both driven over this GATT channel as written. Hardware details the app code could not show: the characteristic's properties byte is 0x28 — write + INDICATE, so server→client messages are ATT Handle Value Indications (the client must confirm them), not notifications; the stack tolerates an unconfirmed-then-confirmed mix, and the CCCD reads 0x0002 on a fresh connection (indications on by default). GATT layout observed: service at handle 0x28, declaration 0x29, VALUE handle 0x2A, CCCD 0x2B. MTU 515 negotiates cleanly. A KEYED unit rejects cleartext writes with ATT application error 0x87 (intermittent, load-dependent) and never answers them.

client_rendering.description: A command's `body` carries only the STATIC envelope fields — `cmd`, plus `data` when the command writes state. The renderer (dispatched on protocol_handler "rabbit_air_lan") supplies the two runtime fields itself: `id` (a fresh client nonce) and `ts` (the device-clock timestamp, learned via the time_sync command and extrapolated from the local clock — see handshake). It then serializes the envelope {id, cmd, ts, data} as minified JSON in that field order (data last, omitted when the body carries none), encrypts with AES-128-CBC under the 16-byte user key using PKCS7 padding and a random 16-byte IV APPENDED as the last 16 bytes (ciphertext || IV), and sends the result as ONE datagram to UDP port 9009 on the device's IP. Responses arrive as one datagram, decrypt the same way (IV = last 16 bytes), and are matched to the request by `id`. `id` and `ts` must never appear in a command body — they are per-send values, and a body that froze them would replay one nonce and one stale timestamp forever.

commands.description: Returns the device clock: response data.ts (seconds). Must precede the first authenticated command.
commands.name: time_sync

commands.description: No `data` in the request. Response data carries the full state object (see state_fields).
commands.name: state_get

commands.description: Request includes `data` with only the fields to change (see writable_state_fields). Changing speed while in Auto/Pollen mode implicitly switches to Manual (mode 2) per vendor client semantics — actually the client exposes mode and speed independently; set mode=2 with speed for explicit manual control.
commands.name: state_set

commands.description: Device info: name (Thing ID), mcu (Wi-Fi firmware version), build (firmware build date), mac, time, uptime / mup (motor runtime) / wup (Wi-Fi uptime) / iup (internet uptime) / cup (cloud uptime), fv (main-board firmware), rssi {cur,min,max,avg}.
commands.name: get_info

encryption.applies_to: Both directions, once a user key is set. During SETUP (before a user key exists) the app sends the same envelope in CLEARTEXT with no `ts` field — see setup_commands. The library's tokenless plaintext mode is the same code path.
encryption.iv: Random 16 bytes per message, APPENDED as the last 16 bytes of the datagram (ciphertext || IV). Decrypt: IV = msg[-16:], ciphertext = msg[:-16].
encryption.key: The 16-byte user key (access token), hex-decoded from the 32-character string shown in the app.

example_exchange.description: Reconstructed from the vendor client source; key/IV here are documentation values, not a real device.
example_exchange.wire_note: On the wire each of these is AES-128-CBC(user_key) with PKCS7 padding and a random 16-byte IV appended after the ciphertext.

handshake.description: No connection or session exists (UDP). The only required preamble when a user key is set is clock sync: send cmd 9, read data.ts (device time, seconds), compute the offset against the local monotonic clock, and stamp every subsequent request with the extrapolated device time. The vendor client re-syncs whenever the socket is re-created (any error closes and re-opens it).

request_fields.data: Object; present with fields on state-set, absent on state-get.
request_fields.id: uint32-ish random client nonce, incremented per request (vendor client seeds from SystemRandom 0..0xFFFFFF); response echoes it.
request_fields.ts: Device-clock timestamp in seconds; REQUIRED when a user key is set. Learned via cmd 9, then extrapolated from the local clock (see handshake).

response_fields.error: Present and truthy on failure — vendor client raises ProtocolError.

commands.description: Response data is a RabbitairWireless object: current ssid, security (int), dhcp, ip, mask, gateway, and `networks` — the device's own Wi-Fi SCAN RESULTS, each {ssid, security(int)}. During setup the app re-polls this (up to 15x) until networks is non-empty, then presents the SSID picker. The `security` enum is partially mapped by hardware observation: 3 = WPA2-PSK (every WPA2 network in the verified unit's scan, and the value the successful join echoed). The same reply doubles as join progress: after cmd 1/2, `ip` stays "0.0.0.0" until the unit has associated AND taken a DHCP lease — on the verified unit that took ~4 minutes. The same SSID appears once per visible BSSID (the verified scan listed the target network 3 times) — dedupe before presenting a picker. Post-setup the reply omits `networks` and carries the live ssid/security/dhcp/ip/mask/gateway/dns1/dns2 only.
commands.name: read_network_settings

commands.description: Request data {"ssid": "...", "passphrase": "...", "security": <int>} — security echoed from the cmd 0 networks[] entry (3 = WPA2-PSK verified). The reply is a bare id ack; a wrong passphrase surfaces later (ip stays 0.0.0.0 and the unit never appears on the LAN). Setup-mode only: after the unit has left setup mode this command returns {"id":<echo>,"error":true} (verified).
commands.name: join_network

commands.description: No data. Ends setup mode (closes the setup AP / BLE setup advertising); the unit joins the network given in cmd 1. Bare id ack. Setup-mode only like cmd 1 — error:true after setup (verified).
commands.name: leave_ap_mode

commands.description: GET (no data): response data.name. SET: request data {"name": "..."}.
commands.name: module_name

commands.description: Request data {"type": <int>, "value": "<string>"}. Types: 0 = AWS IoT root CA, 1 = device certificate, 2 = device private key, 3 = HTTPS root CA, 4 = USER KEY (32 uppercase hex chars, generated client-side). Types 0-3 are cloud binding (skip for local-only provisioning); type 4 is the one that matters locally — it lands the shared AES key for all later encrypted traffic. Firmware gate: type 4 needs mcu >= 24 (ESP32) / >= 2.2 (Inventek) — an mcu 2.2.8 unit accepted it (verified); the key it was pushed immediately drove encrypted LAN and BLE traffic.
commands.name: set_certificate

commands.description: Response data {mode (int 0-5), setup (bool)} — verified reply during setup mode: {"mode":5,"setup":true}.
commands.name: get_current_mode

commands.description: Same command as the post-setup get_info, plaintext during setup. Hardware-verified reply shape: data carries name, mcu, build, wifi (Wi-Fi stack version string), mac (the WI-FI MAC — on the verified unit it differed from the BT MAC only in the last octet), time, heap/hmin/stack/clk, uptime/mup/wup/iup/cup counters, flc/ftc/errw. Without the vendor cloud flow, name is "" (no Thing ID is ever assigned) — consumers must not require it non-empty; the mDNS hostname then falls back to "RabbitAir-<WIFI MAC>" (see discovery).
commands.name: get_info (setup-mode notes)

state_fields.error: 0 none / 1 dust sensor / 2 gas sensor / 3 gas+dust / 4 fan low / 5 NFC (filter tag) / 8 hall sensor (panel)
state_fields.filter_type: 0 unknown / 1 ToxinAbsorber / 2 OdorRemover / 3 GermDefense / 4 PetAllergy (from NFC tag)
state_fields.quality: Air quality 0-4 (Lowest/Low/Medium/High/Highest); BioGS units report 1-5 and the library subtracts 1
state_fields.rssi: int — Wi-Fi RSSI averaged over an hour

tcp.framing: 2-byte little-endian uint16 length prefix, then the JSON message; same payload otherwise.

udp.framing: One JSON message per datagram; no length prefix or delimiter.
udp.retry: Vendor client: 3 attempts, 2.0 s timeout per attempt; responses matched by `id`, unrecognized datagrams ignored.

rabbit_air_protocol.verification_notes: `reported`, leaning on an unusually strong source: the reference is the vendor's own published library plus its Home Assistant integration, cross-checked against the Rabbit Air 2 app binary. Field-name strings in its Dart snapshot match the state model: particulate_sensor, filter_life, filter_timer, filter_ctl, filter_cleaning, filter_replacement, filter_type, timer_mode, all_light_off, lsens_ctl, moodlight, light_sensor, pm_sensor, ionizer, buzzer, quality, schedule, plus the user_key / thingName credential pair. The encryption block is likewise corroborated: the app bundles package:encrypt (AES) and pointycastle with CBC mode and PKCS7 padding — the same AES-CBC/PKCS7 construction the vendor library implements. Not replayed against hardware in this project — no Rabbit Air unit was available.

writable_state_fields.filter_life: int minutes remaining, range guard 0-525600 in the vendor client
writable_state_fields.filter_timer: int nominal filter lifetime (minutes), same range guard
writable_state_fields.moodlight: 0 Off / 1 On / 2 Auto (alias Preset1) / 3 Preset2 / 4 Preset3 — MinusA2 mood light
writable_state_fields.schedule: 24-char string, one per hour UTC, chars '1'-'5' (speed) or 'A' (auto); vendor client validation also admits '0'
writable_state_fields.speed: 0 SuperSilent (read-only, auto modes only) / 1 Silent / 2 Low / 3 Medium / 4 High / 5 Turbo
